units.title: Cost models, asymptotic notation and cases
outcomes: Translate an input bound into a cost budget: state which complexity classes fit n up to 5000, 10^5 and 10^9.
Define Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta with quantifiers, and prove a polynomial bound such as 100x^2 = O(x^2) from the definition.
Derive time and auxiliary-space bounds for nested and input-dependent loops, naming the variable each bound is in.
units.why: Every later choice in this stage starts by reading the constraint line. A wrong budget rejects a working algorithm before it is written, or accepts one that cannot finish.

next.note: Amortized bounds reuse the same definitions with the average taken over a sequence.
Arrays are the first structure whose operations you cost with this vocabulary.

study.title: Computational complexity and Big-O
study.locator: What complexity actually means; How to read a complexity bound (the five notations); The hierarchy you will meet with the input-size table; Space-time tradeoffs

study.title: Mathematics for Computer Science, Chapter 13, Section 13.7
study.locator: Section 13.7 Asymptotic Notation (printed pp. 528 to 549): 13.7.1 Little O, 13.7.2 Big O with Definitions 13.7.5 and 13.7.9 plus Proposition 13.7.10 (100x^2 = O(x^2)), 13.7.3 Theta with Definition 13.7.13, 13.7.4 Pitfalls, 13.7.5 Omega with Definitions 13.7.15 and 13.7.16

study.title: Complexity Models
study.locator: Classical Complexity Theory and Asymptotic Complexity: the instruction-count model and where it breaks (clock speeds and instruction latencies)

study.title: Programming Languages and constant factors
study.locator: Interpreted languages, Compiled Languages and Takeaway: the pure-Python versus C versus OpenBLAS matrix-multiply comparison
study.depth: Read for the constant-factor warning only. Algorithmica's timings are C++ measurements; do not carry any crossover point to Python without your own timeit run.

focus: Constraints are budgets: n up to 10 admits anything, 10^5 admits O(n log n) or better, 10^9 admits O(log n), a closed form or a lookup.
The equality in f(n) = O(g(n)) is one-way: n = O(n^2) holds and the reverse is nonsense.
Worst case is the default reading of complexity; average, expected and amortized each need their own argument, supplied by later units.
Constants are invisible in the notation: the handbook plans Python at about 10^7 simple ops per second against 10^8 for compiled languages.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write the c-and-n0 definitions of O, Omega and Theta and prove 100x^2 = O(x^2). Then time both Two Sum variants at n = 2000 with seed 0 and an absent target in Python 3.13: expect the brute force near 0.04 s per run against the hashmap under 0.2 ms per run, a ratio over 100x on a 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K.
traps: Reading Big-O as an exact operation count. It bounds growth up to a constant, and the constant decides close races.
Quoting the handbook's ops-per-second figures or the n = 50 sort crossover as Python facts. They are compiled-language planning numbers; measure with timeit before repeating them for Python.
Calling one fast observed run an average case. A single input is one sample; an average needs a stated distribution.

selfTest.q: Prove 100x^2 = O(x^2) from the definition.
selfTest.a: Take c = 100 and x0 = 1. For all x >= 1, 0 <= 100x^2 <= 100 * x^2. This is Proposition 13.7.10.

selfTest.q: n = O(n^2) is true. Is n^2 = O(n)?
selfTest.a: No. For every fixed c, n^2 > c * n once n > c, so no constant works. The equality reads one way only.

selfTest.q: A problem allows n up to 10^9 on a one-second budget. Why is a linear scan rejected before coding?
selfTest.a: A billion items cost a full second at one nanosecond each before any real work, and a real scan takes ten to thirty seconds. Only O(log n), a closed form or a lookup fits.

selfTest.q: A dynamic-array push is O(1) amortized. Does that bound the slowest single push?
selfTest.a: No. The push that triggers a resize copies every element, which is O(n). Amortized averages over the sequence; latency-critical code cannot use the average.

practice.name: LeetCode 1: Two Sum
practice.locator: Implement the O(n^2) brute-force double loop and the O(n) complement hashmap. Time both with timeit at n = 2000, seed 0, target absent: expect about 0.04 s per brute run against under 0.2 ms per hash run. State both bounds with the named variable n.
practice.note: After submitting, read the handbook hash-maps section LC 1: value-to-index map for the lookup-then-insert order that avoids matching an element with itself on inputs like [3, 3].

units.stopWhen: You prove a polynomial Theta bound from the definitions without notes, and your Two Sum timing shows the predicted gap with both bounds stated.

fit.note: The handbook chapter plus MIT Section 13.7 cover all three topics at explain and derive depth, and LeetCode 1 gives checked practice.

units.title: Aggregate, accounting and potential amortized analysis
outcomes: Distinguish worst-case-per-operation from amortized cost over a sequence, and name which one a latency-critical loop needs.
Derive the b/(b-1) per-push bound for geometric growth from the series, and compute copy totals for b = 2 and b = 1.125.
Prove binary-counter and dynamic-array bounds by the summation, taxation and potential methods, including the Phi = 2num - capacity derivation.
units.why: Appends, queue transfers and table resizes all hide rare expensive steps inside cheap sequences. Without amortization you either over-reject a fine structure or ship a latency spike.

next.note: Table resizing reuses the same doubling proof with the load factor as the trigger.
The two-stack queue is the next amortized argument.

study.title: Amortised analysis (inside Computational complexity and Big-O)
study.locator: Amortised analysis: the aggregate, banker and potential methods on the dynamic-array example, plus the hard-real-time caveat
study.depth: Read only this section; the rest of the chapter belongs to the previous unit.

study.title: Dynamic array internals
study.locator: The proof in one paragraph (geometric series to b/(b-1)); How fast capacity actually grows (the 1000-push copy counts for b = 2 and b = 1.125); Five libraries (the CPython 1.125 row with the listobject.c formula and the python-dev history); What happens on the way down (shrink hysteresis); the Python-doubles and front-insertion warnings

study.title: Lecture 9: Amortized Analysis, Sections 9.1 to 9.3
study.locator: 9.1 Incrementing a Binary Counter; 9.2 Counting from 0 to n with 9.2.1 Summation, 9.2.2 Taxation, 9.2.3 Charging and 9.2.4 Potential (amortized cost 2 per increment); 9.3 Incrementing and Decrementing (the double-binary counter)
study.depth: Skip 9.4 Gray codes and 9.5 curiosities; they are depth material for later.

focus: Every method answers one question: total cost of the sequence divided by its length. Summation counts flips, taxation banks credit, potential tracks Phi.
The proof needs geometric growth: with factor b the copies sum to at most n/(b-1); arithmetic growth collapses to Theta(n) per push.
CPython grows lists by about 1.125x after the small-list steps 0, 4, 8, 16: about nine moves per push, the highest constant in the table, chosen to bound peak RAM.
Shrinking needs hysteresis (shrink at a quarter full, not a half) or alternating push and pop replays the resize forever.
units.reproduce: Without notes, derive the amortized bound both ways: the copy series summing to at most n/(b-1), and the potential Phi = 2num - capacity with the resize case (k+1) + (2-k) = 3. Then append 200 ints to a list in Python 3.13.14 and confirm with sys.getsizeof that capacity steps land at lengths 1, 5, 9, 17, 25 and 33.
traps: Amortized O(1) does not bound the single slowest push; the resize push copies everything.
Python lists do not double. The formula is (newsize + (newsize >> 3) + 6) & ~3 after the 0, 4, 8 start.
Halving on pop breaks the bound; only the quarter rule (or no shrinking) keeps it.

selfTest.q: Derive the amortized cost per push for growth factor 2.
selfTest.a: Resizes copy 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 = n - 1 elements; plus n slot writes the sequence costs 2n - 1, so at most 2 per push. The potential method with Phi = 2num - capacity gives the looser constant 3; both are O(1).

selfTest.q: In the potential proof, why is the resize push amortized 3 and not k+1?
selfTest.a: Actual cost k+1 plus the Phi change. Before the push the table is full so Phi = 2k - k = k; after, num = k+1 and cap = 2k so Phi = 2. The change is 2-k and the amortized cost is (k+1) + (2-k) = 3.

selfTest.q: How many bit flips do n binary-counter increments from zero perform, exactly?
selfTest.a: 2n minus the number of 1 bits in n. Bit i flips every 2^i iterations, so it flips floor(n/2^i) times.

selfTest.q: Push then pop alternately at the half-full boundary with a halving shrink policy. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Every operation triggers a full resize, so n operations cost Theta(n^2). Shrink only at a quarter full.

study.title: Sliding window: fixed size (invariant-in-code example)
study.locator: The pattern (build-first-window then slide) and the four primitives table
study.depth: Read only the pattern and primitives as the invariant written in code; the full chapter belongs to the two-pointer unit.

focus: An invariant has three obligations: true at the start, preserved by each step, and strong enough to imply the answer at the end.
The oracle must be too simple to share the bug: brute force against optimized, with independent code paths.
derandomize (or a fixed seed) makes the run replayable; shrinking then minimizes the failure, which you map back to the invariant clause.
State the invariant in one sentence before the loop; the window primitives show the shape.
units.reproduce: Write test_window.py comparing the sliding-window max-average against the O(nk) brute-force oracle with Hypothesis lists of ints in [-100, 100] up to length 30 and k in 1 to 30, max_examples=200, derandomize=True. Run under pytest in Python 3.13 with Hypothesis 6.169.0 and pytest 9.1.1: expect 1 passed. Then break the slide step once (drop the minus term) and confirm the test fails on a shrunken input.
traps: Testing the optimized code against itself by reusing its helper in the oracle. The oracle shares the bug and everything passes.
Random tests without seed control: a failure you cannot replay is a rumor, not a regression test.
Showing maintenance without checking that the invariant implies the postcondition at termination.

selfTest.q: State the Invariant Principle in one sentence.
selfTest.a: If a predicate holds initially and every transition preserves it, it holds in all reachable states (Definitions 5.4.4 and 5.4.5).

selfTest.q: Why does the max-average oracle use the O(nk) double loop instead of a second window implementation?
selfTest.a: The double loop recomputes each window from scratch, so it cannot share an off-by-one in the slide update. Independence is what makes disagreement evidence.

selfTest.q: Hypothesis reports a failing input of length 24. What do you do before touching the code?
selfTest.a: Let it shrink, replay the minimal case with derandomize, and identify which invariant clause the minimal input violates.

selfTest.q: Write the invariant for the fixed-size window slide.
selfTest.a: Before each step, s equals the sum of the current k elements. Each step emits the current window and advances by exactly one, so at termination every window was emitted.

practice.name: LeetCode 643: Maximum Average Subarray I
practice.locator: Solve with the build-first-window slide. Commit a Hypothesis differential test against the O(nk) brute force alongside the solution; judge with the worked example nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4], k = 3.
practice.note: After submitting, re-read the handbook sliding-window-fixed worked example and check your trace emits the same running maxima.

units.stopWhen: Your committed test replays deterministically, catches the seeded minus-term bug, and you can point at the invariant line the shrunken input breaks.

fit.note: No pool resource teaches property and differential testing, so the Hypothesis docs enter as a support reference beside MIT Section 5.4; the handbook supplies the invariant-in-code example.

units.title: Arrays, strings, locality and linked structures
outcomes: Implement in-place array routines (compaction, back-merge, rotation) with exact index bounds.
Implement singly linked insert, delete and traversal with a sentinel, and state the pointer invariant.
Explain list over-allocation and string-builder costs from CPython behavior and your own measurements, and separate Python locality from C++ cache numbers.
units.why: Arrays and linked nodes are the two physical layouts everything else composes. Index discipline and pointer discipline learned here prevent the off-by-one and aliasing bugs of every later unit.

next.note: Hash tables layer probing and chaining over the array layout.
Stacks and queues pick their backing layout from this unit.

study.locator: list_resize: the (newsize + (newsize >> 3) + 6) & ~3 formula with the growth-pattern comment (0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76, ...)
study.depth: Read the function and its comment only; the rest of the file is later.

study.title: Cache Lines
study.locator: 64-byte cache lines and the strided-loop demonstration (stride 1 against stride 16)
study.depth: These are C++ measurements on contiguous arrays. Do not quote them for Python lists; your Reproduce shows why.

study.title: External Memory Model
study.locator: Cache-Aware Model and Array Scan: why a scan is the cheapest access pattern
study.depth: Read for the model only; the numbers are C++ measurements.

focus: In-place means bounded extra space with exact bounds: merge from the back, compact with a write pointer, rotate with three reverses.
The sentinel (dummy head) removes the empty-head special case; every rewiring snapshots next before clobbering.
CPython lists over-allocate geometrically (about 1.125x) but store pointers: consecutive elements are separate heap objects, so stride effects differ from C arrays.
Unaliased local string accumulation grows in place on CPython 3.13 and runs near join speed; aliasing (keeping every prefix) restores the quadratic.
units.reproduce: Run the concat script with 30000 distinct parts on Python 3.13.14 (12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K): the aliased prefix-keeping loop takes about 0.8 s while the single-live-reference loop and join each take about a millisecond, a gap over 100x. Then, without notes, implement remove-element compaction plus sentinel-based insert-after and delete-after.
traps: Iterating to capacity instead of length; capacity is uninitialized slack.
Front insertion or pop(0) in a loop: geometric growth amortizes the tail only, so n front inserts cost Theta(n^2).
Quoting the handbook's 2.2x concat figure or Algorithmica's stride numbers as your Python behavior. Both were measured elsewhere; rerun on 3.13.
Rewiring curr.next before saving it: the rest of the list is gone.

selfTest.q: Why does Merge Sorted Array merge from the back?
selfTest.a: The tail of the destination is free buffer. Writing forwards would overwrite unmerged elements; writing backwards only touches buffer cells or already-placed cells.

selfTest.q: Argue the three-reverse rotation correct.
selfTest.a: Reversing everything puts each element at its rotated mirror position; reversing the first k and the rest then fixes each segment's internal order.

selfTest.q: getsizeof steps land at lengths 1, 5, 9 and 17. What capacities are those?
selfTest.a: With a 56-byte header and 8 bytes per slot, 88, 120, 184 and 248 bytes mean 4, 8, 16 and 24 slots, matching the 0, 4, 8, 16, 24 pattern.

selfTest.q: Consecutive list elements sit 32 bytes apart by id(). Why does the stride-16 demo not apply?
selfTest.a: The list stores pointers; elements are separate heap objects. Striding the list still chases pointers, unlike striding a C array of inline values.
